title: A Ledger for the Typewriter
premise: In 1914 Marseille, Marguerite Delacroix, a former soldier living quietly as a woman to escape a court-martial, drives for the suffragist Madame Aubert and reads every letter that passes through her hands. When war is declared and the census taker Armand Vasseur begins asking questions about a German-born typist who vanished from the city's records, Marguerite realizes the woman—Liesl, to whom he once promised safe passage—is trapped behind enemy lines of paperwork and suspicion. Keeping his promise means forging census entries, risking exposure of both his identity and Madame Aubert's network, and trusting the very official hunting Liesl. The story ends with Marguerite surrendering his forged ledger to save Liesl's life, accepting arrest, while Madame Aubert's found family of typists and drivers smuggles the truth—and Liesl herself—to neutral Switzerland.
about_author: Gideon Vane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in provincial French municipal records. He writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Introduces his double life: driver by day, reader of other people's letters by night, a man living as a woman since deserting the army in 1909. He measures belongings by what fits in one suitcase. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness mistaken for safety.

chapters.title: Madame Aubert's Salon
chapters.summary: Marguerite drives Madame Aubert to a suffragist meeting where typists copy petitions in secret. He notices Liesl Brandt, a German-born typist with ink-stained fingers, watching him watch her. POV alternates briefly to Liesl. Beat: the first crack in invisibility—being seen.

chapters.title: A Promise in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through present: two years earlier, Liesl caught Marguerite reading her mail and, instead of exposing him, asked him to read hers. They sealed a pact—he would carry her out of France if war ever came. Beat: intimacy built on mutual secrets.

chapters.title: The Guns of August
chapters.summary: War declared. Marseille fills with reservists and suspicion of all things German. Liesl stops appearing at the salon. Marguerite's POV, frantic but outwardly calm as he drives Madame Aubert through cheering crowds. Beat: dread arriving faster than news.

chapters.title: The Census Taker
chapters.summary: Armand Vasseur, meticulous census official, arrives at Madame Aubert's house with questions about household members past and present—including 'the German girl.' Marguerite lies smoothly for the first time and hates how easily it comes. Beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Letters Undelivered
chapters.summary: Marguerite searches the salon's letter archive and finds Liesl's unsent letters to a sister in Strasbourg, revealing she's hiding in the Panier district under a false French name. Beat: hope rekindled, guilt ignited—he stopped looking too soon.

chapters.title: Vasseur's Ledger
chapters.summary: Vasseur's POV. He cross-references census entries and finds an anomaly: three addresses listing a 'Marguerite Delacroix' with conflicting details. He doesn't yet suspect gender or loyalty—only error, which offends him professionally. Beat: the hunter introduced as a man of order, not malice.

chapters.title: The Panier at Night
chapters.summary: Marguerite navigates the old quarter's stairways to find Liesl working in a print shop under the name Marie Lambert. Their reunion is wary—she knows what his discovery could cost them both. Beat: relief braided with terror.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Liesl refuses to flee without her printing press plates, evidence of the salon's pacifist pamphlets that would condemn everyone if seized. Marguerite argues for the suitcase rule; she argues for the truth. Beat: the promise meets its first price.

chapters.title: An Error in the Record
chapters.summary: Vasseur interviews Marguerite formally. Under gentle questioning, Marguerite nearly slips about dates, and Vasseur notes his hands shake. A neighbor mentions 'the driver who used to be someone else.' Beat: the noose drawn by ordinary diligence.

chapters.title: Madame Aubert's Choice
chapters.summary: Madame Aubert discovers Marguerite's secret visits to Liesl. Instead of dismissing him, she reveals her own buried past—a brother shot as a deserter—and joins the conspiracy. Beat: found family consolidating around shared damage.

chapters.title: Forged Entries
chapters.summary: Marguerite forges census corrections creating a clean paper trail for 'Marie Lambert,' using skills learned forging his own identity for five years. Liesl teaches him the typewriter's rhythm so documents match. Beat: competence as love language.

chapters.title: The Raid on the Print Shop
chapters.summary: Soldiers raid the Panier shop hunting sedition. Marguerite arrives minutes late; the plates are gone—seized by Vasseur as 'evidence.' Liesl escapes through the rooftops but is now visibly hunted. Beat: rising action turns desperate.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Candlelight
chapters.summary: Vasseur studies the seized pamphlets and recognizes the salon's typography. His POV: he suspects treason but hesitates, because his own son died at the front and the pamphlets ask only for peace. Beat: the antagonist's conscience complicates the hunt.

chapters.title: A Bargain Refused
chapters.summary: Vasseur privately offers Marguerite a trade: Liesl's location in exchange for silence about his identity. Marguerite refuses, and Vasseur, unsettled by his own offer, gives him until the week's end before filing charges. Beat: moral stakes crystallized.

chapters.title: The Suitcase Rule Broken
chapters.summary: Liesl agrees to leave without the plates after learning Marguerite plans to confess in her place. They pack together in near-silence, each trying to memorize the other. Beat: tenderness under sentence of separation.

chapters.title: The Night Train Problem
chapters.summary: The plan: Liesl hidden among Madame Aubert's Red Cross supplies bound for the Swiss border. But the departure moves up 24 hours—the same hour Vasseur scheduled his final interview. Beat: clock ticking audibly.

chapters.title: Confession
chapters.summary: Climax part one. Marguerite walks into Vasseur's office and surrenders the forged ledger, confessing everything—desertion, identity, forgery—to buy time for the convoy to reach the border. Vasseur listens, then burns nothing and signs nothing. Beat: sacrifice freely chosen.

chapters.title: Border Lights
chapters.summary: Liesl's POV aboard the convoy, unaware of Marguerite's bargain, recognizing a checkpoint officer as Vasseur's clerk—who waves the vehicle through. She crosses into Switzerland carrying only the letters Marguerite once read. Beat: release through another's unseen mercy.

chapters.title: The Cell and the Key
chapters.summary: Marguerite awaits court-martial in custody, but Madame Aubert mobilizes her network: petitions, a deputy's intervention, testimony that the 'sedition' was humanitarian aid. Vasseur files his report omitting the ledger's most damning page. Beat: grace arriving from every direction at once.

chapters.title: What the Census Missed
chapters.summary: Marguerite is released—charges reduced to administrative error, his secret intact because a dozen people chose to keep it. He returns to the empty salon and finds Liesl's final letter, posted from Geneva: an address, and the word 'whenever.' Beat: grief transmuted into future.

chapters.title: A Ledger Kept Open
chapters.summary: Epilogue, spring 1919. Marguerite, still Marguerite by choice now rather than necessity, drives refugees instead of suffragists, keeping a new ledger—not of names to hide, but of people to find. The last entry is a train number and a date. Beat: identity as ongoing act, memory as promise renewed.
